title: Fourier series: building a repeating sound from simple waves
summary: Say what harmonics are and list them from F₀; explain why any repeating wave is a sum of harmonics; read a series in cosine form, cos+sin form and complex form and convert between them; find coefficients by eye using the 'detector' idea; draw the magnitude spectrum.
sourceNote: fourier_series.pdf (note + slides), Ladefoged (1996) ch. 10, Lab 4. Rewritten in plain steps: one idea per card.

sections.heading: The big idea: any repeating sound is simple waves added up

blocks.md: **You are on step 3 of the map.** Chapter 0 said a vowel is a recipe of simple waves. This chapter says exactly **which** simple waves, and how to find how much of each.
blocks.label: why

blocks.md: **The claim (Fourier's idea).** Take any wave that repeats, like a vowel. You can build it **exactly** by adding simple cosine waves, as long as you use the right ones in the right amounts.

blocks.caption: Fourier synthesis, one harmonic at a time: sines at F₀ (amplitude 1), 3F₀ (1/3), and 5F₀ (1/5), and their sum: already close to a square wave after three terms. Each extra odd harmonic straightens the flats and sharpens the corners; the sharpness lives entirely in the high harmonics, which is why cutting the highs (a phone line, a heavy low-pass) rounds sounds off. Hover any row.
blocks.slide: Three harmonics building a square wave

blocks.caption: Add harmonics one at a time and watch the square wave form; the stems below are the one-sided magnitude spectrum, each labelled with A_k. Switch to triangle to see why 1/k² amplitudes converge so fast, and play each.

blocks.md: Try it in the sim: with 1 wave you get a plain cosine. Add the 3rd and 5th and it starts to look square. The more you add, the closer it gets. Sharp corners need the highest ones.

blocks.prompt: True or false: to build a square wave you need infinitely many simple waves, but a few already get close.
blocks.answer: True. Each extra one sharpens the corners a little more.

sections.heading: Harmonics: which simple waves are allowed

blocks.body: How many times per second the whole wave repeats. For a voice, that's the pitch. Its period is **T₀ = 1 / F₀**.
The simple waves you're allowed to use: whole-number multiples of F₀. **1·F₀, 2·F₀, 3·F₀, …** The k-th harmonic is at **k·F₀**.

blocks.title: Listing harmonics
blocks.body:
F₀ = 100 Hz  →  harmonics at 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 Hz, …
F₀ = 5 Hz    →  5, 10, 15, 20, 25 Hz, …

The 5th harmonic of 5 Hz is at 5 × 5 = 25 Hz.
The period of a 5 Hz wave is 1/5 = 0.2 s.

blocks.md: **Why only multiples?** A wave at 3·F₀ does exactly 3 full repeats in the time the whole sound does 1. So it 'fits' the repeating pattern perfectly. A wave at 2.5·F₀ wouldn't line up at the end of each repeat, so it can't be part of a sound that repeats every T₀.

blocks.prompt: A vowel has F₀ = 120 Hz. Where are its first four harmonics?

sections.heading: Three ways to write the same recipe

blocks.md: You'll see the Fourier series written three ways. They say the **same thing**; they just package the numbers differently. Learn form 1 first. Forms 2 and 3 are for the math and the code.

blocks.title: Form 1: a list of cosines (the friendly one)
blocks.body:
x(t) = A₀ + A₁·cos(2π·1F₀·t + ϕ₁) + A₂·cos(2π·2F₀·t + ϕ₂) + …

Each harmonic k gets its own amplitude Aₖ and starting angle ϕₖ.
A₀ is a constant: the average level of the wave.

Example: x(t) = 0.4 + 1·cos(2π·2·t + π/4) + 0.6·cos(2π·5·t − π/2)
  A₀ = 0.4;  harmonic at 2 Hz: A = 1, ϕ = π/4;  at 5 Hz: A = 0.6, ϕ = −π/2
blocks.slide: Form 1: cosines with A and ϕ

blocks.title: Form 2: a cosine part and a sine part (no ϕ)
blocks.body:
Aₖ·cos(… + ϕₖ)  =  aₖ·cos(…) + bₖ·sin(…)

  aₖ = Aₖ · cos ϕₖ
  bₖ = −Aₖ · sin ϕₖ      (watch the minus)

Back again:  Aₖ = √(aₖ² + bₖ²)

Example: aₖ = 3, bₖ = 4  →  Aₖ = √(9 + 16) = 5

blocks.title: Form 3: complex spinners (what numpy gives you)
blocks.body:
Each cosine = two spinners (Chapter 4), at +k and −k:

  Xₖ = (Aₖ / 2) · e^{jϕₖ}      X₋ₖ = the conjugate of Xₖ

Back again:  Aₖ = 2 · |Xₖ|,   ϕₖ = angle of Xₖ

Example (Lab 4 Q7): 2·cos(2πF₀t + π/2)
  X₁ = (2/2)·e^{jπ/2} = 1·j = j,   X₋₁ = −j

rows: aₖ = Aₖ cos ϕₖ,  bₖ = −Aₖ sin ϕₖ
blocks.title: Conversions cheat sheet

blocks.body: Forgetting the factor of 2 between Xₖ and Aₖ. A cosine of amplitude 4 has |Xₖ| = 2. If a spectrum looks half as tall as expected, this is why.

blocks.prompt: A harmonic has A = 6 and ϕ = 0. What are a, b and Xₖ?

sections.heading: How to find how much of each harmonic: the detector

blocks.md: Given a wave, how do you find its recipe? The idea is like a **radio tuner**: tune to one station and you hear only that station, even though all stations are in the air at once.

blocks.body: To measure harmonic k: **multiply** the wave by a test wave at frequency k·F₀, then **average** the result over one repeat. You get a big number if the wave contains that harmonic, and **zero** if it doesn't.

blocks.md: **Why unmatched harmonics give zero:** a wave times a different harmonic goes up and down evenly, so its average over one repeat is 0 (every hump above the line is canceled by a hump below). Only a harmonic times itself stays mostly positive and survives. The official word for this is **orthogonal**: different harmonics don't interfere with each other's measurement.

frames.caption: Lab 4 Q9. A wave made of two cosines: one at F₀ (amplitude 2) and one at 3F₀ (amplitude 3). Question: how much of each harmonic is in it?

lines: the F₀ part matches → keep it
the 3F₀ part doesn't match → averages to 0
frames.caption: The 'detector' for harmonic 1 only responds to the F₀ part. Everything else cancels out.
The two-sided coefficient is half the amplitude (Chapter 4: a cosine is two half-size spinners). Phase is 0, so X₁ = 1.
Neither part is at 2F₀, so the detector finds nothing.

lines: test for harmonic 3: the 3F₀ part matches
frames.caption: Only the second cosine responds. Half its amplitude: 1.5.

lines: change the 3F₀ amplitude to 6 → X₁ is still 1
give the 3F₀ part phase π/2 → X₃ = 1.5·e^{jπ/2} = 1.5j
frames.caption: Q10 and Q11: changing one harmonic never affects the others' coefficients. Amplitude goes into the size of X, phase into its angle.

blocks.title: The formulas (for reference)
blocks.body:
a₀ = (1/T₀) ∫ x(t) dt                        the average
aₖ = (2/T₀) ∫ x(t) · cos(2π·k·F₀·t) dt
bₖ = (2/T₀) ∫ x(t) · sin(2π·k·F₀·t) dt
Xₖ = (1/T₀) ∫ x(t) · e^{−j2π·k·F₀·t} dt

All integrals over one period (0 to T₀). '∫ … dt' ÷ T₀ just means 'average over one repeat'.

blocks.prompt: x(t) = 5·cos(2π·10·t) + 2·cos(2π·20·t) with F₀ = 10 Hz. What is X₂ (two-sided)?
blocks.answer: Only the 20 Hz part matches harmonic 2. Amplitude 2, phase 0 → X₂ = 2/2 = 1.

blocks.body: A plot with a vertical line (a 'stem') at each harmonic frequency, as tall as that harmonic's amplitude Aₖ.

blocks.title: Lab 4's triangle wave, F₀ = 5 Hz
blocks.body:
Amplitudes: Aₖ = 8/(π²k²) for odd k, and 0 for even k.

  k = 1 at  5 Hz: 8/π²      ≈ 0.81
  k = 2 at 10 Hz: 0
  k = 3 at 15 Hz: 8/(9π²)   ≈ 0.09
  k = 5 at 25 Hz: 8/(25π²)  ≈ 0.03

Stems at 5, 15, 25, 35, 45 Hz, shrinking fast. Nothing at 10, 20, 30, 40.

Right: its magnitude spectrum: stems at the odd harmonics of 5 Hz with amplitudes 8/(π²k²), and exact zeros (red) at the even ones. The first stem towers over the rest because of the 1/k² decay, yet without the tiny high stems the corners would round off. Hover any part.
blocks.slide: The triangle wave and its spectrum

blocks.md: **What the spectrum tells you about a voice:** the **spacing** of the stems is F₀ (the pitch). The **pattern of heights** is the timbre, which for speech means the vowel. Change the spacing and you change the pitch; change the heights and you change the vowel.

blocks.prompt: x(t) = 4·cos(2π·10·t − π/3). Draw the one-sided magnitude spectrum.
blocks.answer: One stem at 10 Hz, height 4. (Two-sided: stems at ±10 Hz, height 2 each.)

exercises.title: Coefficients by eye
exercises.prompt: x(t) = 3 + 4·cos(2π·10·t) + 2·cos(2π·30·t + π/2). What is F₀? Give A₀, and the amplitude and phase of each harmonic. Then give X₁ and X₃.
hints: F₀ is the biggest frequency that both 10 and 30 are whole multiples of.
Read A and ϕ straight off each cosine; the constant is A₀.
solution: A₀ = 3. Harmonic 1: A = 4, ϕ = 0. Harmonic 3: A = 2, ϕ = π/2. Harmonic 2: 0.
exercises.why: This is Lab 4's block of questions, done without any calculus.

exercises.title: Why the detector ignores other harmonics
exercises.prompt: In one or two sentences: why does multiplying by cos(2π·F₀·t) and averaging ignore a cos(2π·2F₀·t) part of the wave?
hints: What does cos(F₀) × cos(2F₀) look like over one repeat?
Is it more above the line or below?
What's the average of something that's equally above and below?
solution: The product of two different harmonics goes up and down evenly over one repeat, so its average is zero. Only the matching harmonic (cos × cos of the same frequency) stays positive on average.
exercises.why: The same 'multiply and average' trick runs Wi-Fi and 5G: each channel's detector ignores all the others.
